messages.subject: simple mixture model puzzle
parts:
Hello,

I'm learning Stan and working through a simplified version of the already simple mixture model in the manual by fixing the mixture coefficients and standard deviations.  Apparently I'm not getting convergence.  Am I missing something obvious?  Thanks in advance for any insights!

# set up simulated data
N=1000
K=4
c <- sample(1:4, N, replace=TRUE)
# set the true means
mu=c(-10.,0.,10.,20.)
s = 1:N
for (i in 1:N){
  s[i] = rnorm(1, mu[c[i]], .25)
}
data = list(N=N,K = K, y = s)

Here is the model:

data {
  int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
  real y[N]; // observations
}
parameters {
  real mu[K]; // locations of mixture components
}
model {
  real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities
  mu ~ uniform(-30,30);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      ps[k] <- log(.25) + normal_log(y[n],mu[k], .25);
    }
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
}

The call:

fit = stan(file='mixTest.stan',data=data,iter=10000,chains=4)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simple mixture model puzzle
parts:
I think you win the R-hat bowling league --- I've never
seen an Rhat of 300!

1. You are probably getting low R-hat because of label switching.
because which component is which is not identified. See the problematic
posteriors chapter of the model for some possible solutions.

2. Because you have mu ~ uniform(-30,30), mu should be declared
with real<lower=-30,upper=30>. Stan models require support on all
parameter values matching the constraints. Or you could leave mu
unconstrained and use an improper uniform prior. This actually looks
like it could be a problem given where your mu is sampling.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simple mixture model puzzle
parts:
That's surprising given the normal prior. I'd try making the
prior tighter. Also, you probably want log(1.0 / K) rather than log(0.25)
if you want it to just be a uniform mixture. But you don't even need
a constant there, because

log_sum_exp(a + b, a + c)

= log(exp(a + b) + exp(a + c))

= log(exp(a) * exp(b) + exp(a) * exp(c))

= log(exp(a) * (exp(b) + exp(c))

= a + log(exp(b) + exp(c))

and the constant term a doesn't do anything for sampling because we only
need the density up to a constant (unless you care about your joint log
probability function f(y, theta | x) [y modeled data, theta params, x predictors]
being normalized as the value of lp__).

- Bob

I just had to play with this myself --- I should've done
that before putting the example in the manual. Bottom line
is that Seth's absolutely right --- it's a multimodality and
local optimum problem. I'll add some hedges to the manual for the
next release:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1420#issuecomment-111238073

I think the problem you're going to run into is with random inits or
initial steps getting too close to each other, so reasonable inits with
a smaller initial step size will probably help things settle down.

The deeper problem is that there's not going to be enough properly
directed energy in HMC's random momenta to get out of a local
optimum (Metropolis will have the same problem, and there will not be
enough freedom in the conditional samples to move in Gibbs, either).

So if you can do meaningful inits, that'd be a huge help in
this case where there are local optima to fall into. Of course,
you won't get complete mixing in your posterior if you don't consider
the degenerate solutions, but I'm guessing their mass will be negligible
compared to the "correct" solution, so it probably won't matter.

One approach is to use many more mixture components than you think your
data needs --- if two go to the same place, it's probably no big deal in
terms of the overall posterior density.

You get another problem when you estimate sd in that there
are degenerate unbounded likelihood solutions when one of the
sigma goes to 0 and the mean for that cluster approaches the value
of a single item in the data set.

- Bob

No, it doesn't. It's calculated param by param, but does
use cross-chain information and it does split each chain in
half, which is why it's more conservative than what you get in
say Coda. The definition's in BDA3 and in the Stan manual.

- Bob

> On Jun 12, 2015, at 7:18 AM, Mark Ettinger <jetti...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Thanks to all for looking into this. I'm not an expert in MCMC, just trying to use Stan, so I'm not sure I understand the subtleties here. Is it correct to say that the conclusion is that this is still an identifiability problem? If so, why isn't the problem resolved by declaring the means to be an ordered data type? Should this not eliminate multimodality?

It eliminates the label swapping, but not the more degenerate multimodality
you get when two components collapse onto each other.

For instance, consider what happens if you really have two mixture components
but fit it with a model with five. It's likely that a bunch of those mixture
components are going to be close to each other.

But even in the case where the model matches the generative process, you
get local optima of the likelihood with collapsed modes.

Suppose I have two components that are (near) identical and at the same
mixture component:

mu[1] ~=~ mu[2]
sigma[1] ~=~ sigma[2]

Then if you look at the derivative of the log likelihood, it goes down
as mu[1] moves away from mu[2]. You can do the log likelihood plot if you want with
everything fixed other than mu[1] to see the problem.

Now if the valleys are steep enough, as they are in your very well
separated example, the problem is that if you initialize or initially
jump randomly to a place where mu[1] is close to mu[2], there's not enough
energy to get away in the algorithm. Same problem that you run into using
classical optimization techniques looking for a maximum likelihood estimate.

In higher dimensions, the normal mixture turns into K-means clustering,
which is very multimodal and combinatorially impossible to optimize
properly. So it's not just MCMC, it's the fundamental nature of computing :-)

- Bob
